title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 23: Lumanlaw v. Peralta: Violation of the Right to Speedy Trial
keywords: illegal possession of a dangerous drug
primary_topics: Chapter 23 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Lumanlaw v. Peralta, a unanimous ruling penned by the Chief Justice holding that an accused detained for almost two years through fourteen postponed arraignments had been denied his right to speedy trial and could compel the dismissal of the Information by mandamus.

The Court's test for delay: the 30-day period of the Speedy Trial Act is not absolute, and rather than making mathematical calculations of elapsed periods one must ask whether the delays were vexatious, capricious, oppressive or unjustified.

The judicial-administration lesson drawn from the case: an arraignment takes at most ten minutes, a judge should have appointed a counsel de oficio when the accused himself asked for one, and efficient supervision of the clerk of court would have ensured timely service of produce orders on the jail wardens.

The remedial holding: mandamus lies to control the exercise of discretion where undue delay amounts to grave abuse resulting in manifest injustice, and procedural objections such as the want of a motion for reconsideration and the hierarchy of courts yield when constitutional rights are at stake.
sub_topics: Lumanlaw was charged with illegal possession of a dangerous drug in November 2002 and detained in the Manila City Jail by virtue of a Commitment Order.

From his arrest in 2002 to the filing of the Petition in 2004 his arraignment was postponed fourteen times -- for the absence of his counsel, the judge's unavailability, and the warden's failure to bring him to court -- leaving him detained almost two years without arraignment, and both of his Motions to Dismiss were denied.
He filed a Petition for Mandamus under Rule 65, arguing that the failure to act expeditiously on his arraignment violated his right to speedy trial and justified dismissal of the charge.

On the first issue the Court held the violation manifest, given the length and unreasonableness of a majority of the delays and the lack of earnest effort to conduct the arraignment as soon as the calendar allowed.

It observed that an arraignment is a simple but fundamental stage -- reading the charges, ensuring the accused understands them, and taking his plea -- that a prudent and resolute judge can conduct as soon as the accused is presented.

The absence of counsel de parte was no valid reason to postpone, especially where the accused himself asked for a counsel de oficio; refusing that request was unreasonable, without legal basis and attributable to the judge's inflexibility as regards contingencies.

The foremost cause of delay was the repeated failure of the jail wardens to produce the accused, a problem that efficient court management and supervision of the clerk of court could easily have averted.

The judge had allowed the listlessness of the parties, his staff and the wardens to dictate the pace of the proceedings, and had exerted no effort to expedite matters even after two urgent Motions to Dismiss.

On the second issue the Court held that mandamus may issue to control the exercise of discretion where undue delay constitutes grave abuse resulting in manifest injustice, and is available to an accused to compel dismissal of a case.

The general rule requiring a prior motion for reconsideration was held not impervious to exceptions, and the Court refused to deny the writ on purely technical grounds -- including the hierarchy of courts -- where a party would be deprived of substantive rights.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 23 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Lumanlaw v. Peralta, a unanimous ruling penned by the Chief Justice. Lumanlaw was charged with illegal possession of a dangerous drug in November 2002 and held in the Manila City Jail under a Commitment Order, yet his arraignment was postponed fourteen times between his arrest and the filing of his Petition in 2004 -- because his counsel de parte was absent, because the judge was unavailable, and above all because the jail wardens repeatedly failed to bring him to court -- leaving him detained almost two years without ever being arraigned, his two Motions to Dismiss both denied. He sought mandamus under Rule 65. The Court held his right to speedy trial violated, explaining that the 30-day period of the Speedy Trial Act is not absolute and that judicial proceedings must contend with the realities of everyday life, so the question is not a mathematical calculation of elapsed periods but whether the delays were vexatious, capricious, oppressive or unjustified. Reviewing the reasons for each postponement, it found the violation manifest and saw a lack of earnest effort to arraign the accused as soon as the calendar allowed. It observed that an arraignment takes at most ten minutes and entails no legal gymnastics, that the absence of private counsel was no reason to postpone when the accused himself had asked for a counsel de oficio, and that the wardens' failures could have been averted by efficient court management and proper supervision of the clerk of court. The judge had instead let the listlessness of the parties, his staff and the wardens dictate the pace, doing nothing even after two urgent Motions to Dismiss. On the remedy, the Court held that mandamus may issue to control discretion where undue delay amounts to grave abuse producing manifest injustice, and that the want of a prior motion for reconsideration and the hierarchy of courts would not bar the writ, since procedural rules are not strictly enforced when enforcement would cause a miscarriage of justice and the protection of the people's civil liberties overwhelms all rules of procedure.
